newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin sets top government priorities for 1997.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin sets top government priorities for 1997.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin told his government on Tuesday that military reform, payment of wage arrears, protection of domestic industries and health care should be the top priorities for the rest of this year.

A Kremlin press release said Yeltsin had met Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and his two first deputies, pro-market liberals Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov, to review the first six months of 1997 and set future targets.

The government said it had met Yeltsin's demands and paid off a huge backlog of pensions to elderly Russians by Tuesday, clearing one of the first major hurdles since being reshuffled by Yeltsin in March in a bid to kick-start stalled reforms.

Chernomyrdin said on Monday the next priority would be the armed forces, where discontent is rife over non-payment of salaries and general decline. He said he had been instructed by Yeltsin to pay all debts to the army in July and August.
The Kremlin said Yeltsin had told the government on Tuesday to pay wage arrears to servicemen within two to three months.
Chubais said on Monday that debts to the military totalled five 5 trillion roubles ($865 million) and would be paid in three or four months.
Russian news agencies said Yeltsin had opened his meeting with the ministers at a state residence near Moscow with a question over the situation in the troubled Far Eastern region.
About 300 employees of the Zvezda nuclear submarine servicing plant broke through police barriers and blocked the Trans-Siberian railway for about two hours on Tuesday.
Police in riot gear tried to prevent the workers, who say they have not been paid for 10 months, from blocking the tracks but there were no clashes.
Yeltsin reshuffled the cabinet dramatically in March, putting reformers like Chubais, 41, and Nemtsov, 37, into key posts under the more conservative but loyal Chernomyrdin.
Yeltsin had called the previous cabinet "stagnant" and gave the new one strong support in its efforts to put state finances in order, reorganise natural monopolies and fight corruption.
The cabinet now needs some public successes, like payment of state debts to pensioners, servicemen and others on the state payroll, to make reforms more acceptable to disgruntled citizens.
But it says it is meeting opposition from the State Duma lower house of parliament.

The Duma went on holiday last week until September 1 after rejecting cabinet proposals to cut 1997 budget spending across the board because of revenue shortfalls, and to slash some social benefits -- a legacy of Soviet paternalism the government says it can no longer afford.
Yeltsin and Chubais, both known for a tough line towards the Duma, have said the government will pursue its policy regardless of whether it has the legislature's backing.

But Chernomyrdin took a slightly more conciliatory line on Monday, saying the cabinet needed the Duma's support and promising to try to persuade deputies to interrupt their holiday and consider the most pressing draft bills in July.

The head of the Duma, Gennady Seleznyov, told reporters after meeting faction leaders that convening a special session might be possible, but only if the government revised its original plans -- a clear reference to the Duma's earlier requests that spending cuts be limited.
Chernomyrdin met Seleznyov later on Tuesday but there were no immediate details of the meeting.
Seleznyov has accused the president of illegal nepotism for appointing his own daughter as his official Kremlin image-maker.
He said Monday's decree naming 37-year-old Tatyana Dyachenko adviser to the president contradicted the law on Russia's civil service, a bill approved by parliament and by Yeltsin himself.
Also on Tuesday, Yeltsin sacked communist Aman Tuleyev as Minister of Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) Affairs and appointed him governor of Siberia's Kemerovo region.

Tuleyev, effectively the last representative of the opposition in the government, is highly popular in Kemerovo and is seen as a favourite to win a governorship poll in October. ($ = 5781 Russian Roubles)
